Chapter 7: Lessons Learned—and Forgotten
After every big accident, there’s this burst of activity, right? Investigators rush in, everyone’s writing reports, and all sorts of promises are made. For a little while, it really does feel like things are going to change. Maybe a new procedure gets rolled out, equipment gets upgraded, and people spend more time training. But then, slowly, the sense of urgency fades away. People move on, budgets get tighter, and those hard-earned lessons? They start to slip through the cracks.
There’s a story that sticks out—a group of officers who nearly had a disaster on their hands. Shaken, they push for better safety rules. They spend months collecting data, drafting memos, and meeting with the folks in charge. For a while, it looks like they’re actually making progress. But then, something else grabs everyone’s attention—a new crisis, a new priority—and just like that, their recommendations get quietly pushed aside. The officers are frustrated, but honestly, they aren’t surprised. It’s not the first time this has happened.
This cycle—learning after a scare, forgetting as time passes, and then having to relearn the same old lessons—runs all through the history of the nuclear arsenal. Every generation faces its own emergencies, makes its own mistakes, and then tries to patch things up. But the fixes? They’re usually just temporary, and the same issues keep popping up again and again, just wearing a different disguise.
It’s so easy to fall into the trap of thinking, “Hey, this new technology will finally solve everything,” or, “These new procedures will make us bulletproof.” But you and I both know it’s never that simple. The system is constantly changing, and with every change, new vulnerabilities show up. The people in charge, no matter how hard they try, always seem to be a half-step behind.
Here’s something to pay attention to: real safety doesn’t come from quick technical fixes. It takes a culture built on honesty, humility, and constant vigilance. That means questioning what we think we know, being open to tough conversations, and always—always—learning from the past. Without that, we’re just setting ourselves up to repeat the same mistakes, over and over again.
